object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier onboarded by procurement to provide goods/services; recorded in the supplier master.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master.
Oh. Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: Legal Name
object_types.definition: The legal name of a vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really

object_types.name: Tax ID
object_types.definition: A tax identification value recorded for a vendor; not unique across vendors.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really
We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together

object_types.name: Vendor Status
object_types.definition: The lifecycle status of a vendor record.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended.
Collapsed into three, yes. Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.

object_types.name: Spend Tier
object_types.definition: Procurement's classification of a vendor by spend level.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with

object_types.name: Risk Tier
object_types.definition: Compliance's classification of a vendor by risk level, derived from the risk review.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review

object_types.name: Risk Review
object_types.definition: A record of a compliance risk assessment performed on a vendor, over time; only one may be current/signed-off.

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

object_types.name: Region
object_types.definition: A geographic sourcing region in which a vendor may operate.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM.

object_types.name: Contact
object_types.definition: A named contact person acting as the primary contact for a vendor in a particular region.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.

object_types.definition: The email address of a contact.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.

object_types.name: Contact Phone Number
object_types.definition: The phone number of a contact.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.

object_types.name: Purchase Order
object_types.definition: A request raised against a vendor to purchase goods/services.

source_references.excerpt: A purchase order has a PO number. That's its identifier, same idea as vendor number.

object_types.name: Amount
object_types.definition: The monetary amount of a purchase order.

source_references.excerpt: It has an amount and a raised date.

object_types.name: Raised Date
object_types.definition: The date a purchase order was raised.

source_references.excerpt: It has an amount and a raised date.

ambiguities.description: Dana initially states informally that vendors are told apart 'by name, usually' before the facilitator clarifies system-level identification is by vendor number. This hedge ('usually') suggests name-based confusion may exist informally even though vendor number is the formal identifier.

source_references.excerpt: How do you tell one vendor from another? -- By name, usually.

ambiguities.description: Dana initially claims the tax form (W-9) on file is the gate for a vendor to become active/transactable, but Raj contradicts this, stating the actual system rule (since March) requires a completed and signed-off risk review, not just the tax form. It's unclear whether the W-9 is still a mandatory precondition alongside the review, or was fully superseded — the transcript resolves the status-transition rule but does not clarify whether tax documentation remains a separate required gate.

source_references.excerpt: Tax form on file. Once the W-9 is in, they're live and a buyer can raise a PO. ... A vendor cannot be moved to active until a risk review has been completed and signed off.

ambiguities.description: 'Tier' is used ambiguously by different stakeholders to mean two different fields (spend tier: bronze/silver/gold, owned by procurement; risk tier: low/medium/high, owned by compliance/derived from review). Both are colloquially called 'tier' causing confusion in the business, though the system models them as two distinct fields. This is flagged explicitly by the facilitator as unfinished/parked business ('I want to come back to this because I don't think we've finished it') though it does get resolved later — however the naming ambiguity in real-world usage (people saying 'tier' without qualifying spend/risk) remains a business communication problem not solved by the data model.

source_references.excerpt: And you both call it 'tier.' ... We've asked people to say spend tier and risk tier. Nobody does. It's been a losing battle for two years.

ambiguities.description: The 'preferred vendor' notion tracked in Mei's informal spreadsheet is explicitly declared ad hoc and out of scope for modeling, per Mei's own instruction ('It's ad hoc. Don't model it.'). This is a deliberate gap, not a rule, and is called out as such rather than silently omitted.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called 'preferred.' ... It's ad hoc. Don't model it.

ambiguities.description: The rule for what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended (halt immediately vs. a proposed 'run-off' status) is explicitly left undecided, pending a policy decision by the sourcing steering group and Legal. No fourth vendor status is agreed upon, so the current three-status model (draft, active, suspended) may be incomplete pending this future decision.

source_references.excerpt: My position is that everything halts immediately. ... I'm not agreeing to a fourth status in this room, off the cuff, without Legal. ... what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate vendor records (same tax ID, same company onboarded twice) are acknowledged as a known, longstanding, unresolved data quality/compliance problem, explicitly marked out of scope for this session but not something the model can currently prevent or detect via tax ID since it's not unique.

source_references.excerpt: We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them. ... Noted, but out of scope for today.

ambiguities.description: The final exchange establishes a precise read-back of the model, but it's unclear whether 'vendor operates in region' is a distinct fact from having a primary contact in that region, or whether 'operating in a region' is only inferable from the existence of a primary contact record (i.e., no explicit vendor-region operation fact/flag was described independently of the contact assignment).

source_references.excerpt: And can a vendor have no contact in a region? -- If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all.
